To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
X4-trophic and dual-tropic viruses were transmitted vertically in 5 mother-infant pairs, and that these viruses were not derived from the R5-tropic strains in the infants.

(1) X4-tropic (T-tropic) HIV-1 can infect and be transmitted to newborn infants; (2) dual-tropic viruses can infect and be vertically transmitted to infants; and (3) the X4-tropic virus populations are genetically similar to the X4-tropism virus populations in the mothers.
X4-using viruses were found to be transmitted from mother-to-infant in five Ugandan infants, and the viruses were either transmitted perinatally, or arose shortly after birth.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular and immunological basis for the development of HIV-1 infection and disease in infants and children.
the development of new HIV-1 vaccine strategies.
the transmission and early pathogenesis of HIV infection in infants in sub-Saharan Africa.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the X4-tropic viruses found in the infants were transmitted from their mothers, either at or before delivery, or within 6–8 weeks after delivery, and that the CXCR4-tropism of these viruses was not due to a genetic change in the V3 loop.
the infants in this study had acquired HIV-1 perinatally, and the virus populations in these infants were derived from their mothers.
the infants’ CXCR4-using virus is a vertical transmission of the mother’s virus, not a de novo emergence in the infant.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the majority of HIV-1-infected infants in Uganda harbor CXCR4-using variants, and that these variants were transmitted vertically from the mother.
we have shown that CXCR4-using variants can be transmitted from mothers to infants, and that the transmission of CXCR4 using variants is not a rare event.
we found that HIV-1 is capable of infecting the placenta, and that this infection can lead to the transmission of CXCR4-tropic HIV- to the fetus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
X4-using viruses are transmitted from mother to child and that these viruses are not necessarily the same as those that are transmitted from child to child.
X4-trophic HIV can be transmitted from the mother at the time of birth or in utero.

HIV-1 is transmitted in a complex manner that involves multiple routes of infection, and that it is transmitted as a heterogeneous population of viruses that can evolve to become more virulent and transmittable.
